121stoneandalliehood.title: #121: The Lord’s Prayer Around the World with Stone and Allie Hood
121stoneandalliehood.body:
On this episode of Missions Pulse, David Joannes sits down with Stone and Allie Hood, a married couple traveling the world to film believers praying the Lord’s Prayer in their own languages, a dream that began in a Hawaii dorm room ten years ago.

 📖 If this conversation stirs something in you, you can follow Stone and Allie’s journey, pray for them, and learn more about The Lord’s Prayer Project as they travel from nation to nation. 

Stone was twenty and studying at Kauai Bible College when a picture hit him on the walk back to his dorm: a wide variety of believers praying the Lord’s Prayer in their own language and culture, bouncing from person to person. He was overwhelmed. He ran to his room, journaled it, and felt a press to capture it. He bought a GoPro, later upgraded to a Sony, and signed up for the World Race, eleven countries in eleven months along the 10/40 Window. It seemed like the perfect chance. It didn’t work. Filming believers across a language barrier felt off, and Stone realized he was so focused on finishing the project that he wasn’t letting it change him. The dream went quiet for years.

Allie’s road ran through a different kind of waiting. She graduated from the University of Tennessee ready to sell everything and go anywhere, and God sent her to a corporate job in Denver instead. Stone followed her there and became a youth pastor. About a year into their marriage, he shared the dream with her, and she had an “aha moment”: this was what God had asked her to wait for. They held it for a couple more years until they felt a yes.

Those seasons reshaped how they pray. Allie says her prayers in the corporate job were mostly cries for help, which was beautiful, but she wasn’t good at listening and had no burning passion for intercession until God challenged her to notice how many of Jesus’ prayers were for others. Stone, as a youth pastor, ran into the Barna finding that the average pastor prays about five minutes a day and admitted it described him. He had realized he could do a lot without God, and “how scary that is.” The Lord’s Prayer, they say, can become hollow when we’ve known it all our lives.

David presses into what he calls a privatized faith, citing a 2013 Barna report that 51 percent of North American churchgoers don’t know what the Great Commission is. Stone and Allie agree that prayer is both a private pursuit and a corporate one, and they point out that the prayer begins with “our.” Prayer, they say, is absolutely missional: it starts with who God is, then moves to His kingdom come and His will be done. Allie shares how Luke 10:19 has fired her up to pray big, bold prayers, and how joining prayer sets in different countries has stretched her heart far beyond herself.

The heart of the conversation is a night in South Korea. Stone and Allie had no connections there but felt pressed to go. After a prayer set at a church, they felt no push to film the welcoming believers, even though they would have said yes. At the train station they discovered a cash-only kiosk, and they had just spent their last won at a Goodwill. They wondered if they should go back. Instead, they stopped and surrendered to God right there. Not even twenty seconds later, a Korean couple who had seen them praying walked up and asked in great English if they needed help. The man, Young, ended up saying the Lord’s Prayer in Korean, on camera, in the subway station. “This can only be you, God,” Stone says.

So far the trip has taken them through Japan, South Korea, and Thailand, with Indonesia, Kenya, and Estonia on their hearts, though they don’t know where they’re headed from one week to the next. The finished video will bounce clip by clip from English to Chinese to many other tongues, running perhaps two to four minutes. Along the way they’re asking believers three questions: What is prayer? How can someone live a devoted prayer life? How can the nations pray for your country? David adds a language lesson of his own, noting that the Chinese version of “Our Father” runs backwards, with “our” and “above the heavens” coming before “Father.” He ties it all to Revelation 7:9, where every tribe and tongue stands before the throne, with more than 17,000 languages and thousands of unreached people groups still waiting to hear.

Stone and Allie expect to finish filming in December and release the video on Instagram and their website in January or spring, though they’re walking open-handed. The conversation ends with Stone and Allie praying for anyone who feels stuck on the sidelines of God’s great dream, asking the Holy Spirit to teach all of us to pray.

This episode reminds us that prayer is the doorway into God’s heart for the nations. The invitation to know God’s heart and join His mission is still open.

120davehatfield.title: #120: From Beverly Hills Stockbroker to Missionary in Kenya: Dave Hatfield’s Story
120davehatfield.body:
On this episode of Missions Pulse, David Joannes connects with Dave Hatfield, founder and president of Livingstone Global, who joins from Nakuru, Kenya. Dave never set out to be a missionary. He was a Beverly Hills stockbroker who gave his life to Christ at 46, and nineteen years later he is still saying yes to the next thing God puts in front of him.

📖 If this conversation stirs something in you, you can learn more about, pray for, or give to the work of Livingstone Global at livingstoneglobal.org.

Dave describes himself as an “American dream kid.” He made his goal lists, listened to Zig Ziglar, and had accomplished everything on them by 35. Then life got dry. When his business partner took the business, the identity he had built around success went with it. Not long after, he walked into a church in a small town, heard the gospel for the first time, and realized he had been following the wrong playbook. Seven months later he took a ten-day trip to Kenya with his 13-year-old son. The day school let out, he went back with his wife and their ten-year-old, because he couldn’t explain what God had done in his heart and they needed to see it for themselves.

What began as a short-term trip became a school. Dave saw three- and four-year-old children with nowhere to go until age seven, and the problem solver in him said, “Let’s open a preschool.” They started with 18 children. A few years in, a partnership fell apart, funding was pulled, and the school closed. Dave had quit in his heart. Then God said something he did not expect: “Do it again, and I’ll be with you.” He had $273, no land, and three months. In January the doors opened with 18 children again. Today Maisha Mapya, which means “new life” in Swahili, serves over 400 students through grade nine. Many of them call him “Daddy Dave,” and Dave is careful about what that means. In a place with few healthy father figures, he says, it is a chance to point children to their Heavenly Father. David adds Amy Carmichael, known as Amma to the children of Dohnavur, as another picture of a missionary who became family.

The heart of the conversation is what happened during COVID. Tensions between rival groups in the community were rising, and a four-year-old student’s family was caught in the middle. Dave was locked down in California when God told him, “Go to Nakuru and I’ll make peace between the groups through you.” He was 59, with no seminary and no training. He went. He ended up baptizing two rival members in the same water after they asked each other for forgiveness. Word spread, and people began bringing him their hardest problems. One by one, men who had lived by violence gave their lives to Christ.

What came next was just as unusual. A former group leader named Wes told Dave he wanted to do something for God. Dave suggested they read the Bible together, and Wes said, “Right now.” They opened the book of John on the steps where Wes used to spend his days. Within nine days, 32 people were coming. For three years Dave taught and Wes translated, then the two traded places, because it was Wes’s church and Wes’s people. They called it Light and Love Church, and it still has no programs, no membership, and no offering, just tea and an hour in the Word. They later rented a bar and turned it into a coffee shop where free coffee, open Bibles, and prayer meet people where they are. Dave says it was never about fixing the community. It was about staying. “I was the one who didn’t leave,” he says, through a staff betrayal, the loss of the school, and the hardest seasons.

Dave also shares what he calls the biblical case for short-term missions. In Mark 4, Jesus tells his disciples to cross to the other side of the lake. The point, Dave says, was to form them: to put them in unfamiliar situations they couldn’t control and see what came out. He tells visitors to just come, without a perfect plan, and let God shape them. David connects this to his own story, since a short-term trip at 14 set the course for a long-term commitment in his life. For Dave, formation is the whole point. “No one’s changed more than me,” he says, at 65, and God used the people of Kenya to teach him how to follow Jesus. Even the pace of his ministry was part of that formation. Dave wanted to expand years ago, but God told him he wasn’t yet who he needed him to be. After losing nearly his whole team, the staff has been rebuilt to 62, including an American missionary family, and Dave is out of daily operations.

Looking ahead, Dave dreams of turning a five-acre property into a boarding school and building a Christian restoration home for women on land that borders Lake Nakuru National Park. Six men from Wes’s former group now work with Livingstone Global after going through an eight-month Bible-based program. Dave is also writing a trilogy about the call, the cost, and the life he is living now. He knows his next step of faith is to step back so the ministry belongs to the community. He and his wife, Kim, are volunteers who don’t draw a salary, and Dave is the organization’s only fundraiser. David closes the conversation by encouraging listeners to visit livingstoneglobal.org and to find Dave’s books there or on Amazon.

This episode reminds us that obedience doesn’t have to be complicated. Say yes, take the next step, and stay. The invitation to know God’s heart and join His mission is still open.

119johnnyyeverino.title: #119: Ruined for the Ordinary: Johnny’s Journey from a Dream to Thailand
119johnnyyeverino.body:
On this episode of Missions Pulse, David Joannes sits down in Chiang Mai with Johnny Yeverino, a young missionary whose road to Thailand started with a dream when he was fifteen and took a decade of detours, closed doors, and surrender to reach.

📖 If this conversation stirs something in you, you can pray for, connect with, or learn more about the work of Within Reach Global in Chiang Mai as Johnny steps into this next season. 

Johnny was born in El Paso, Texas, and raised across the border in Juárez, Mexico, where his parents still do ministry. In high school he began dreaming about Thailand: green mountains, preaching the gospel to children and youth, a Bible study in a house with his future wife in the kitchen. He knew nothing about the 10/40 Window or the persecuted church. He just told his parents he thought he was going to be a missionary. By sixteen he was leading youth in his parents’ church, and during COVID he moved to a large church in El Paso where he worked full-time in youth ministry. It looked like the place he was meant to stay. But God kept telling him he would step back from everything to truly know His heart. Then a stranger from a visiting Christ for the Nations team prayed over him and said almost exactly those words.

Within weeks he was enrolled at Christ for the Nations Institute in Dallas. “The Lord just ruined my heart for anything ordinary,” Johnny says. Every semester he wanted to buy a one-way ticket somewhere hard, and every semester God slowed him down. David points out that this two-sided coin keeps showing up in missions stories: identity and destiny, sonship and sending. Johnny saw the contrast clearly in Thailand’s Buddhist culture, where people work constantly to correct their karma, and in the church, where Christians often do the same thing. God, he says, wants our wholeness first. The works flow from that.

The heart of the conversation is a moment in a house of prayer. Twice, doors to Thailand had closed. Then came a month in Turkey and Kazakhstan that gave Johnny a deep burden for Muslims, and he planned his whole last semester around a one-way ticket back. During worship, God asked him a question that undid him: “Would you surrender Turkey?” Johnny was angry and heartbroken. Then he felt God telling him to look at His hands, which had given him dreams and nations, and then to look at His face. “He’s the goal. He is the mission.” Johnny realized he had been gripping the gifts instead of the Giver, and the story of Abraham and Isaac came to mind. David adds Amy Carmichael, who was turned away by Hudson Taylor’s China Inland Mission and rerouted through Japan and Sri Lanka before she reached the children of South India. Years later she wrote to them: “He kept me for you, my darlings.”

What came next was just as unusual. Johnny spent forty days in prayer fasting from questions, asking God for nothing and simply being with Him. Midway through, a team from Taiwan visited his school. By the end of the forty days he had peace and everything he needed for the trip, and he spent six months in Taiwan. For two and a half years God had also been repeating five things to him: a house of prayer, a coffee shop, the 10/40 Window, the persecuted church, and next-generation discipleship. He knew nothing about Within Reach Global when he reached out. Days before a visa run to Thailand, someone answered. They told him to meet at a coffee shop that turned out to be part of the ministry. It has a house of prayer on the fourth floor and sits across from a college campus, where the team disciples young adults and intercedes for the 10/40 Window. The team had already received a vision of Johnny. “I was mind blown,” he says.

Johnny’s advice to a fifteen-year-old with a stirring in their heart is simple. Don’t ignore the tug, and keep the fire burning by learning the state of the global church. Take small, practical steps, like a short-term trip or a Bible institute. And let God purify your heart along the way, because “God doesn’t steer a parked car,” as David puts it. Looking ten years ahead, Johnny doesn’t know where he’ll be. He does know he wants to work with the persecuted church and the unreached, raising up worshipers and disciples who will sing the songs of the Lord boldly in places the Word hasn’t reached. David links this to the Moravians, whose hundred years of unbroken prayer in 1727 launched a missions movement, and to Revelation 7:9, where every tribe and tongue worships because Jesus is worthy of the reward of His suffering.

This episode reminds us that a calling is a person before it is a place. Johnny closes with a challenge in Spanish to the Mexican church: learn about the persecuted church and the unreached, and respond to the Great Commission, because Mexico can send missionaries too. The invitation to know God’s heart and join His mission is still open.

118kendallcobb.title: #118: A Legacy of Faith: Kendall Cobb on His Family's Lifelong Missionary Journey
118kendallcobb.body:
On this episode of Missions Pulse, David Joannes sits down with his longtime friend Kendall Cobb, a second-generation missionary whose story begins on a freighter ship in 1966 and is still unfolding today in Chiang Mai, Thailand.

📖 If this conversation stirs something in you, you can pray for, partner with, or give toward the work of Bible Way and ActsCo Printing as they move into this next season. Learn more here.

Kendall is the son of the late Alvin Cobb and has spent his whole life in missions. He serves as Bible Way Asia Director and as Co-Founder & Director of ActsCo Printing, a Christian printing ministry in Thailand that has served more than 8,000 clients since opening its doors in 1999.

Kendall was four years old when his family boarded the SS Robin Goodfellow in New York City, bound for Madagascar. The voyage took 52 days, 17 of them without sight of land, and it was full of the kind of stories only a missionary family collects: brothers dangling over the ship's railing, a crocodile bite, a locked cabin door, and a little boy listening to gospel stories on LP while sitting in a pulled-out dresser drawer. "It just became a part of life," Kendall says. "I never knew any different." That, David suggests, is how missions becomes a family's DNA rather than a short season.

From Madagascar, the story moves like chapters of a book you can't put down. After a revolution, Alvin prayed that God would open a door to West Germany. The next day a letter arrived inviting him to take over a pastorate. He led a church on a U.S. military base, where eight people grew to a few hundred, and, Kendall says, hardly a Sunday passed without someone accepting Christ. Soldiers who came to faith there eventually planted sixty churches and carried it home. Alvin also rented a 50-room castle for $400 a month and turned it into a Bible training center the family called the Lighthouse.

Then came Hong Kong, and the work of getting Bibles into a China that had barely reopened. Kendall is quick to say his dad never thought of it as smuggling. You put Bibles in bags, he explains, and if they get caught, great, and if not, they get through. Over nine years, Kendall estimates, about 7,000 people came through the ministry, and he distributed roughly 700 tons of Bibles. He tells of a hotel storage room where his father was handed a receipt for one bag and walked out with all of them, of Bibles printed on the "third shift" at state presses, and of a prison warden who printed Bibles on paper so thin you needed black cardboard behind the page to read it. David, who joined the ministry in Hong Kong in 1997, remembers Alvin laughing on a hotel rooftop as he pointed a laser light at people who had never seen one.

What makes the conversation land isn't just the history, though. It's the faith underneath it. Alvin was never hindered by finances. When he believed the Lord had told him to do something, he moved; when it was time to leave the castle, he handed it over with a handshake. That same faith carried Kendall to Thailand in 1998 with no specific plan. He started by duplicating cassettes and Jesus film VHS tapes, and then a quote to print 1.2 million gospel booklets came back too high. His father decided they'd just buy the equipment and print it themselves. That was the seed of ActsCo Printing, which Kendall says became debt-free in 2004 and has never missed a salary. ActsCo Bookhouse, in partnership with Love Packages, has since received more than 150 twenty-foot containers of literature. "Paper between the fingers, the printed word of God will never disappear," he says, especially where the internet can't reach.

Underneath all of it is a quieter point that gives the whole episode its shape: this isn't about a family's legacy; it's about what God sets in motion. Alvin passed away just months before this recording, five months shy of 95, and Kendall's mother is 96 and still living in Thailand. Alvin left behind five acres of debt-free land with an unfinished building, a place that waited for twenty years. The family now believes it's time to develop it into a center for translating, printing, and multiplying the gospel in print and digital form, with a goal of getting a newly translated language into people's hands within a week or two. They call it the 2050 vision. Kendall admits it's "way beyond us," and he repeats his father's favorite line: "We've done so much with so little for so long, we now attempt the impossible with nothing." Then he adds, "That nothing is Jesus."

📖 If this conversation stirs something in you, you can pray for, partner with, or give toward the work of Bible Way and ActsCo Printing as they move into this next season. Learn more here.

This episode reminds us that a legacy isn't something you leave behind so much as something you set in motion and that the invitation is still open. Kendall's charge is simple: don't say yes to God unless you're willing to follow, and never say "send Joe." It's still the greatest adventure there is.

117shanepruittshellymelia.title: #117: Reaching Generation Alpha: Shane Pruitt & Shelly Melia on Real Faith in a Digital World
117shanepruittshellymelia.body:
On this episode of Missions Pulse, David Joannes welcomes two incredible guests: Shane Pruitt and Shelly Melia.

Shane is the Next Gen Director at NAMB and the author of 9 Common Lies Christians Believe, Calling Out the Called, Revival Generation, and Not My Jesus.

Dr. Shelly Melia serves as the Associate Dean of the Graduate School of Ministry and Professor of Childhood Education at Dallas Baptist University. Before DBU, she served as a children's and family minister for over 25 years at churches in Oklahoma, Florida, and Texas. She is also a licensed professional counselor, an editor and contributor for Children and Salvation, and co-authored the newly released book Reaching Generation Alpha with Shane Pruitt.

Shane Pruitt has spent years running diagnostics on youth ministries, and he says the question everyone used to ask — what percentage of our students are being discipled? — is now the wrong question entirely. In this episode of Missions Pulse, Shane and Dr. Shelly Melia, co-authors of the newly released Reaching Generation Alpha: A Ministry Guide for Discipling the Church Beyond the Screen, make the case that every single kid in Generation Alpha is already being discipled. The only question left is by whom — a pop star, an algorithm, TikTok, or the church.

That reframe sits at the center of the conversation. Shelly points out that Gen Z was shaped by technology — social media arrived and changed them. Gen Alpha is different: they're being formed by technology, from the moment mom or dad first hands them a tablet. Add artificial intelligence into that mix, and you get a generation that, according to Shane, doesn't know who or what it can trust anymore — not even its own eyes, since the video might be AI, the image might be generated, the "friend" might be a bot. Into that vacuum, he argues, the church has a strange kind of opportunity: to be the one thing that's still real. Not perfect, not polished, but honest — a community that can be trusted precisely because it admits where it's messy.

Shelly is candid about where that trust has to be rebuilt first: inside the home. She and Shane cite research suggesting parents are largely unaware of what their kids are doing with AI, and unaware of how early exposure to pornography — and the ability to generate explicit content themselves — has crept into ordinary childhood. Her counsel isn't panic; it's presence. Kids don't need a lecture, she says, they need someone willing to sit down and ask, "What questions do you have?" instead of just telling them what to think. Shane's own house rule with his six kids is blunter still: nothing is off-limits, bring us the awkward questions, bring us the "cringy" ones — because if they don't bring them home, they'll go find the answers somewhere else, and "we're probably not gonna like where they go."

What makes the episode land isn't just the diagnosis, though — it's the refusal to let parents off the hook by demanding perfection instead. Shane pushes back hard on the idea that kids need flawless role models. They don't. They need adults who are visibly following someone who is perfect, and who are honest about their own failures along the way. "The greatest thing you can do for your kids," he says, "is to follow the one who is perfect" — discipleship out of the overflow of your own walk with Jesus, not out of guilt for the ways you've already fallen short.

Underneath all of it is a quieter theological point that gives the whole conversation its shape: this isn't ultimately about strategy, it's about identity. Generation Alpha is growing up anxious, over-stimulated, and short on real-world play and grounding — but Shane and Shelly both return to the same hope, that a generation this connected to global peers, this fluent in searching for truth, is not a lost cause but a mission field standing in plain sight. Some of the most spiritually mature people in a household today, Shane notes, are the kids — not the parents.

📖 If this conversation resonates, Shane and Shelly's book, Reaching Generation Alpha: A Ministry Guide for Discipling the Church Beyond the Screen, digs even deeper into the cultural landscape shaping this generation — and what it actually takes to disciple them well. Get it here.

This episode is a reminder that reaching the next generation was never going to look like reaching the last one — but the goal hasn't changed. It's still discipleship. It's just being fought for on a different battlefield.

116gregstier.title: #116: Engage, Not Enrage: Greg Stier on the Art and Heart of Sharing the Gospel
116gregstier.body:
Greg Stier has spent over 30 years teaching teenagers how to share their faith, and he says most of us get one thing backwards: we think the goal of a gospel conversation is to win the argument. It isn't. "The goal is to win the soul," he says — and those are very different skills. In this episode of Missions Pulse, Greg, founder of Dare 2 Share Ministries and author of Radical Like Jesus and Unlikely Fighter, joins us for a conversation about what it actually looks like to share your faith well, not just often.


His framework is disarmingly simple: ask, admire, admit. Ask good questions and actually find out what someone believes. Admire whatever common ground you can find, the way Paul did with the men of Athens. Then admit — tell your own story of needing a savior before you tell God's. Underneath that framework sits a posture Greg borrows from George Whitfield's old prayer for "the mixture of the lion and the lamb": start with the lamb, because a lion's roar scares people off before you ever get there. Only once trust is built does the truth-telling — sin, judgment, the real cost of the gospel — get to do its work.

That posture runs against two temptations Greg spends real time dismantling. The first is treating evangelism as something you live but never say out loud — the well-meaning idea that a good example is enough. Greg calls that flying a plane with one wing. The second is treating faith itself as a ladder to climb, whether it's the five pillars of Islam, the eightfold path, or ten commandments kept well enough. Christianity, he argues, is the only chair in the room — you don't climb it, you rest your full weight on what's already finished. It's a distinction he's watched land in Buddhist villages and American driveways alike.

The most memorable moment in the episode isn't a principle at all — it's his five-year-old son, mid-errand at a grocery store, noticing a grieving stranger Greg himself was trying to hurry past. The boy's unscripted gospel presentation, using nothing but his own hand as a visual, is what finally breaks the woman open. Greg keeps returning to that story not for its drama but for what it exposes: how often the moment to say something is right in front of us, and how often we're too busy to see it. It's the same instinct behind his "prayer, care, and share" model of compassion — help is good, but withholding the actual cure, he says, is like fluffing a dying friend's pillow and leaving the room.

That same conviction scales up into how Greg thinks about discipleship generally, whether raising his own kids or building a ministry now active in over a hundred countries. He'd rather aim for health than numbers, on the theory that a healthy church or family produces growth as a byproduct, not a target. And he's blunt about what happens when that formation is skipped: teaching kids sound theology without ever asking them to open their mouths is, in his words, "pouring milk into a sponge and leaving it there."

This episode is a reminder that sharing your faith isn't a personality trait some people have and others don't — it's a posture that can be built, practiced, and passed down, one conversation at a time.

115davidgarrison.title: #115: Church Planting Movements and the Unreached World: A Conversation with David Garrison
115davidgarrison.body:
At eight years old, in a small Baptist church in southern Arkansas, David Garrison heard the story of the Ethiopian eunuch and asked his parents what was stopping him from being baptized. He couldn't have known then that decades later he'd spend his life chasing that same question — what's stopping the gospel from reaching the people who've never heard it — across more than a hundred countries. In this episode of Missions Pulse, David, author of Church Planting Movements and Wind in the House of Islam and a 31-year veteran of the International Mission Board, joins us for a conversation about what he's seen when the gospel moves fast, and why it so rarely looks the way we expect.

David traces his call back to a single afternoon in a conference room, where a mentor drew a circle on a whiteboard and split it into three parts: the Christian world, the reached-but-not-Christian world, and — at the top — the unreached. That diagram never let him go. It sent him and his family to Egypt, Tunisia, India, Hong Kong, and beyond, documenting what he calls church planting movements: seasons when new believers, often with no missionary in sight, start multiplying churches faster than anyone can track. His first booklet on the subject was meant for a small audience. Instead it spread into 44 languages, and David found himself trying to explain something that had genuinely surprised him — an indigenous momentum he hadn't engineered and couldn't take credit for.

The conversation doesn't stay comfortable for long. David tells the story of Amal, a young Egyptian woman disowned and hunted by her own family after coming to faith, who found peace not in safety but in reading Matthew 10 and realizing Jesus had warned her this would happen. He recounts the death of Mejhanur, a Bangladeshi convert tortured for refusing to recant — and the stranger turn that followed, when two of his killers later showed up at his widow's door, having themselves come to faith, asking to serve the family they'd wronged. These aren't stories offered for shock value; they're the pattern David has watched repeat itself for three decades — persecution as the soil movements often grow in, not the thing that stops them.

The episode also turns to what's happening right now in Iran, where David estimates the number of underground believers is climbing into the hundreds of thousands, largely propelled by women. And running underneath all of it is a challenge to comfort itself — David's own reflection on what he calls "cul-de-sac syndrome," watching his kids invent their own risks in a safe American suburb, and choosing instead to move his family toward difficulty on purpose.

This episode is a reminder that the fastest-growing seasons of the church have rarely been the safest ones — and that the invitation to join what God is doing usually starts, as David puts it, with a simple yes.

114dennismelnichuk.title: #114: Prayer, War, and the Next Generation: A Conversation with Dennis Melnichuk
114dennismelnichuk.body:
Standing in the kitchen with his wife, just days before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Dennis Melnichuk felt a single word settle on both their hearts: come, you need to go out west. They gathered a team, told everyone to bring their passports, and left on what looked like an ordinary missions trip. Three days later the war began, and the roads heading east, toward the people trying to escape, were nearly empty. In this episode of Missions Pulse, Dennis, founder of Awakened Generation and a missionary who moved from China to Ukraine in 2019, joins us from Chiang Mai to talk about what it means to stay when everything says go, and why prayer, not activity, has been the thing that kept him in the fight.

Dennis’s path to Ukraine began with a leap he describes as radical: in June 2019, with little context and no clear plan, he packed up his life in China and went where he felt the Lord leading. He started traveling the country with teams and local partners, visiting churches along the old Donbass front lines, where an evangelical “mega church” once meant about fifty people. When the invasion came, that team helped organize evacuations and pulled thousands of people out of dangerous areas. Today Awakened Generation runs a missions base, a coffee shop, and a prayer room, and hosts conferences and events built for young people. The vision behind it all is simple: before anyone learns to do the works of Christ, they need to know they are a son or daughter first.

The conversation doesn’t stay in the comfortable places for long. Dennis describes the leadership vacuum the war created, with pastors fleeing and men drafted, and the young people who have stepped into it, praying for the sick and preaching in the streets. He admits that during the hardest stretch of the war he burned out so completely that he couldn’t pray at all, and for about three weeks he set an alarm for 5:15 a.m., lay on the floor, and said only “Help me.” He tells of a trip into the Amazon where a group of soldiers, then a line of villagers, came asking for prayer. Host David shares a story of his own, how adopting his daughter in Thailand opened his eyes to what spiritual adoption means. Running through all of it is the idea that mission fueled by urgency alone eventually hardens the heart, and that the prayer room is what keeps a team from becoming a machine.

The episode also asks how this model can travel. Dennis and David compare notes on pairing a coffee shop with a prayer room, a place where non-believers can wander in for an open mic night or a “Bible study for non-religious” and meet people who have just come from the presence of God. Dennis points to the Moravians, whose hundred-year prayer vigil launched one of the largest missions movements in Protestant history, as proof that prayer and action belong together. He names the biggest threat to revival in one word, “ego,” and the biggest obstacle to missions as an unwillingness to relinquish what is comfortable. His own picture of success is a modest one: sons and daughters who become fathers and mothers, and a ministry that eventually doesn’t need him.

This episode is a reminder that the mission is not a project to be managed but a life to be given, and that the road to sacrifice, as Dennis puts it, “leads also to resurrection.”

113johnschlitt.title: #113: The Voice of Petra: John Schlitt on Addiction, Redemption, and Six Decades of Rock
113johnschlitt.body:
In this episode of Missions Pulse, John Schlitt, four-time Grammy Award winner, 10-time Dove Award winner, and lead singer of Petra, joins us for a raw and moving conversation about rock and roll, addiction, and the redemption that changed the course of his life. What began as a garage band with three chords in small-town Illinois grew into decades of touring with Head East and later Petra — but behind the sold-out crowds and chart-topping singles was a darker story of drugs, alcohol, and a marriage nearly lost.

Throughout the episode, John walks through his early years chasing the "musician's dream," the slow spiral into addiction that cost him his band and nearly his family, and the devastating night in 1980 that brought him to the edge. He shares candidly about the five years that followed — years spent away from music entirely, working ordinary jobs and rebuilding his life — before God unexpectedly called him back to the stage through Petra.

This conversation also challenges the idea that ministry only happens behind a microphone or from a pulpit. John reflects on how Petra was received by both the church and the world, the pushback the band faced even from other believers, and why he ultimately stopped performing for approval and started performing for an audience of One. He also opens up about his hands-on ministry work today, helping people in practical, everyday ways.

If you've ever wondered whether your gifts — however unconventional — have a place in God's mission, this episode offers both honesty and hope. From the highs of the touring life to the quiet years of rebuilding, John casts a vision for what it looks like to keep showing up, keep saying yes, and let God redeem even the most broken chapters.

This episode is a reminder that God doesn't waste our past — he redeems it, and uses it for a purpose far bigger than we could imagine.
